**Next: [B] MC08-B04 — Astra:** select the observation algebra, full model, and energy meaning before specifying E07.
I'll need a high level description of results to move forward
I’ll summarize what E06 established and the choices it leaves for the next step.

**We now have an explicit, regular system-plus-environment model that reproduces the theta transfer’s signed amplitudes at any chosen observation time, for every finite cutoff within the established local interval.** This resolves a physical-realization question. The remaining task is to decide what mathematical information this model could expose.

The key change is the clock. Previously, identifying physical time directly with the activity parameter \(v\) produced immediate, linear loss. A system coupled to a fixed vacuum environment through a bounded Hamiltonian initially loses probability quadratically. Those behaviors were incompatible under the earlier assumptions.

Choosing **\(v=at^2\)** makes the transfer’s initial loss quadratic too. E06 checked that this compatibility extends to an actual construction: the joint Hamiltonian stays finite and continuous, including at startup. At a corresponding value of \(v\), the original determinant amplitudes and their signs remain unchanged.

The construction has a concrete interpretation. At each finite cutoff, we add an environment with the same number of fermionic modes as the system. Particles can move between system and environment, while total particle number is conserved. If we inspect the environment at the end and find it empty, the remaining system amplitude is exactly the prescribed theta transfer. A calibrated reference experiment can recover its **sign**, including the necessary success-probability factors.

There are now two available models with different capabilities:

| Model | What it supplies |
| --- | --- |
| Original stream of fresh environment modes | The complete continuous loss-count record, with its established limiting construction |
| New fixed finite environment | A regular driven joint Hamiltonian and exact final vacuum-conditioned amplitudes |

The distinction matters because a particle in the fixed environment can leave the system and return before the final observation. Continuously requiring “no loss has ever occurred” imposes a different condition. We have also left open whether the two models give the same unconditioned endpoint evolution on physical observables.

Three research questions remain:

- **Energy meaning:** the new total Hamiltonian generates the construction, but we have not identified its energies with the theta source levels \(\pi n^2\).
- **Infinite system:** the regularity proof works separately at every finite cutoff; it does not yet establish a regular infinite-system Hamiltonian.
- **Signed estimates:** the construction preserves the desired amplitudes, but provides no new inequality controlling their signs. The known negative polynomial control also admits this generic construction.

**The decision for moving forward is which capability the next argument actually needs:** final signed amplitudes, the complete monitored record, or a Hamiltonian tied more directly to theta source energy. E06 makes the first option concrete; the others carry additional obligations.

**Next: [B] MC08-B04 — Astra:** choose that observation and energy specification, then define one bounded follow-up calculation or proof. The [continuation note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/07_positive_theta_primitives/01_jensen/01_mellin_curvature/08_open_quantum_dynamics/research-progress/handoffs/08_MC08_E06_RETURN_AND_B04_MODEL_CONTINUATION_20261103.md) preserves the details for a model change.

I strongly favor the energy meaning investigation. I think that for the infinite limit understanding the finite energies is provably sufficient (correct me if I'm wrong, supposing you can take the finite limits to \infty). Regarding the signed estimates, that is probably definitively the most difficult part of RH overall, so the only way to attack it is through the alternative "indirect" routes, but again, correct me if I'm wrong.
I’ll distinguish what finite-energy analysis can establish about the infinite limit from what still needs proof, and use your preference to guide the next energy investigation.

A controlled limit of the full finite models can establish the infinite model. Energy levels alone leave out eigenstates and couplings, which affect the amplitudes. One detail matters here: each finite MC08 model already uses the complete theta spectrum; its cutoff limits the coefficient space used to encode the determinants.

**I’ve made energy meaning the priority for the next investigation.** Your finite-first intuition is sound, with an important qualification; your preference for indirect routes is reasonable, but “the only way” is stronger than we can justify.

**A controlled limit of the full finite models can be sufficient.** We need their Hamiltonians, states, couplings and relevant observables to converge in a way that preserves the claim we want. Knowing the energy levels alone is insufficient: two Hamiltonians can have identical energies but different eigenstates and therefore different transition amplitudes. Standard convergence theorems make this precise for time-independent self-adjoint Hamiltonians; our driven model requires additional time-dependent control. [Teschl, §6.6](https://radon.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-schroe/schroe2.pdf)

Thus your phrase “supposing you can take the finite limits” contains a substantive part of the proof. It is a legitimate route, and we can let the finite-energy investigation identify exactly which convergence statement is needed.

One detail specific to our construction matters: **each finite MC08 model already contains the complete theta source.** Its cutoff limits coefficient sites, rather than truncating the square-energy spectrum. Every fixed determinant is represented exactly once its indices fit inside the cutoff. What remains unresolved is how the corresponding joint Hamiltonians fit together as that encoding space grows.

On signed estimates, I agree with pursuing a structural route that makes the desired sign a consequence of something more understandable. An energy principle, spectral correspondence or response identity could potentially do that. But we cannot establish that direct signed analysis is impossible, or rank this formulation as definitively the hardest part of RH.

The indirect route must eventually supply the missing implication:

\[
\text{source-specific energy structure}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\text{the required determinant or zero statement}.
\]

Real energies and positive thermal probabilities alone do not supply that implication. The opportunity is to find additional structure arising from the actual square spectrum and theta identities.

For B04, I would therefore lead with three questions:

1. What do the finite joint Hamiltonian’s energies and energy responses mean?
2. How are they related to the theta source energies \(\pi n^2\) and our signed observable?
3. Which part of that relationship needs an infinite limit?

I recorded this direction and its qualifications in [Note06](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/07_positive_theta_primitives/01_jensen/01_mellin_curvature/08_open_quantum_dynamics/brainstorm/notes/06_ENERGY_PRIORITY_FINITE_LIMITS_AND_INDIRECT_ROUTES_20261103.md).

**Next: [B] MC08-B04 — Astra, energy-first:** identify the useful energy correspondence before choosing the required limit theorem.
I need to see the equations to back up your assertions. I am specifically interested in how the Hamiltonian is constructed.
I’ll derive the Hamiltonian from the prescribed transfer, then show how the finite system–environment Hamiltonian is constructed and how it relates to the theta energy operator.

The construction has two stages. The transfer fixes its reduced coherent Hamiltonian once the basis and clock are chosen. We then choose a unitary completion on a larger space; that choice fixes the total Hamiltonian. The total energy spectrum therefore depends on the completion, so its relation to the theta energies needs a separate argument.

**The Hamiltonian is constructed backwards from the transfer we want to realize.** There are two stages: the transfer fixes a reduced coherent Hamiltonian; choosing a system–environment unitary then fixes a total Hamiltonian. Here are the equations, with \(\hbar=1\).

Fix \(N\ge0\), put \(m=N+1\), and let \(S_N\) be the backward shift on \(m\) coefficient sites. The starting operator is

\[
\boxed{
K_{v,N}=\frac{F(vS_N)}{F(v)}
=\frac{1}{F(v)}\sum_{j=0}^{N}c_jv^jS_N^j,
}
\qquad
c_j=\frac1{(2j)!}\int_0^\infty u^{2j}\Phi(u)\,du.
\]

The denominator \(F(v)=\sum_{j\ge0}c_jv^j\) remains complete. We prescribe this transfer because its fermionic matrix elements are the desired determinants:

\[
\langle I|\Gamma(K_{v,N})|J\rangle
=
\frac{v^{\sum J-\sum I}}{F(v)^r}
\det[c_{j_b-i_a}],
\qquad |I|=|J|=r.
\]

Thus the amplitude requirement comes first.

If \(\psi(v)=K_{v,N}\psi(0)\), differentiation forces its generator:

\[
\psi'=G_N(v)\psi,
\]

\[
\boxed{
G_N=K'_{v,N}K_{v,N}^{-1}
=S_NF'(vS_N)F(vS_N)^{-1}
-\frac{F'(v)}{F(v)}I.
}
\]

This is generally nonunitary evolution. To interpret it as evolution conditioned on no loss, write

\[
\boxed{
G_N=-iH_N-\frac12R_N,
\qquad
H_N=\frac{i}{2}(G_N-G_N^\dagger),
\qquad
R_N=-(G_N+G_N^\dagger).
}
\]

These formulas uniquely separate coherent motion from attenuation. Probability completeness requires \(R_N\ge0\): infinitesimal measurement operators satisfy

\[
M_0=I+G_N\,dv+o(dv),\qquad M_\mu=\sqrt{dv}\,L_\mu+o(\sqrt{dv}),
\]

so

\[
M_0^\dagger M_0+\sum_\mu M_\mu^\dagger M_\mu=I+o(dv)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
R_N=\sum_\mu L_\mu^\dagger L_\mu.
\]

The substantive earlier result was that the actual theta source satisfies

\[
R_N(v)\ge\frac{2I-S_N-S_N^\dagger}{8000}\ge0,
\qquad 0\le v\le\frac1{25}.
\]

For a concrete example, set \(q=c_1/c_0\) and \(\gamma(v)=F'(v)/F(v)\). At \(N=1\),

\[
K_{v,1}=\frac1{F(v)}
\begin{pmatrix}c_0&vc_1\\0&c_0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
G_1=
\begin{pmatrix}-\gamma&q\\0&-\gamma\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Consequently,

\[
\boxed{
H_1=\frac q2
\begin{pmatrix}0&i\\-i&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
R_1=
\begin{pmatrix}2\gamma&-q\\-q&2\gamma\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

This displays the construction explicitly: coherent hopping and loss combine to produce the directed transfer.

With physical time chosen by \(v=at^2\),

\[
\widetilde G_N(t)=2at\,G_N(at^2),\qquad
\boxed{\widetilde H_N(t)=2at\,H_N(at^2)},
\qquad
\widetilde R_N(t)=2at\,R_N(at^2).
\]

The system Fock Hamiltonian is \(d\Gamma(\widetilde H_N)\). Its coherent part alone does not generate the conditioned transfer; the loss contribution is essential.

**The full system–environment Hamiltonian comes from a further choice.** E06 uses \(m\) environment modes and sets

\[
C(t)=K_{at^2,N},\qquad
D(t)=\sqrt{I-C^\dagger C},\qquad
E(t)=\sqrt{I-CC^\dagger}.
\]

It then chooses the joint unitary

\[
\boxed{
U(t)=
\begin{pmatrix}C&-E\\D&C^\dagger\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

The identity \(EC=CD\) proves unitarity, and \(U(0)=I\). Once this complete joint path is chosen, its Hamiltonian follows from Schrödinger’s equation:

\[
i\dot U=h_{\mathrm{tot},N}U
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{h_{\mathrm{tot},N}=i\dot U\,U^\dagger.}
\]

Explicitly,

\[
\boxed{
h_{\mathrm{tot},N}
=i\begin{pmatrix}
\dot C C^\dagger+\dot E E&
\dot C D-\dot E C\\
\dot D C^\dagger-\dot C^\dagger E&
\dot D D+\dot C^\dagger C
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

Here \(\dot C=2at\,G_N(at^2)C\). The square-root derivatives are determined by equations such as

\[
D\dot D+\dot D D
=-(\dot C^\dagger C+C^\dagger\dot C).
\]

Differentiating \(UU^\dagger=I\) proves that \(h_{\mathrm{tot},N}\) is Hermitian. Its many-particle Hamiltonian is

\[
\mathbb H_{\mathrm{tot},N}
=d\Gamma(h_{\mathrm{tot},N})
=\sum_{\alpha,\beta=1}^{2m}
(h_{\mathrm{tot},N})_{\alpha\beta}
f_\alpha^\dagger f_\beta.
\]

Starting the environment in vacuum gives exactly

\[
\boxed{
\langle\Omega_E|\Gamma(U(t))|\Omega_E\rangle
=\Gamma(K_{at^2,N}).
}
\]

That equation connects the full Hamiltonian construction back to the original signed determinants.

The quadratic clock makes the startup Hamiltonian particularly explicit. Since

\[
R_N(0)=q(2I-S_N-S_N^\dagger),
\]

we have

\[
C(t)=I+at^2G_N(0)+O(t^4),\qquad
D(t),E(t)=\sqrt a\,t\sqrt{R_N(0)}+O(t^3).
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
h_{\mathrm{tot},N}(0)=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&-iB_N\\
iB_N&0
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad B_N=\sqrt{aR_N(0)}.
}
\]

It is a finite exchange Hamiltonian, even though \(\widetilde H_N(0)=0\). Its exact one-particle energies are

\[
\boxed{
\varepsilon_{k,\pm}(0)
=\pm\sqrt{
aq\left(2-2\cos\frac{k\pi}{m+1}\right)
},
\qquad k=1,\ldots,m.
}
\]

For \(N=1\), these are

\[
\pm\sqrt{aq},\qquad \pm\sqrt{3aq}.
\]

Fock-state energies are sums over occupied energy eigenmodes.

These equations explain why I distinguished the constructed energies from the source energies. The theta source uses

\[
L_+|n\rangle=\pi n^2|n\rangle,
\]

whereas the displayed joint startup energies depend on \(a\), \(c_1/c_0\), and the selected completion.

Moreover, the completion has explicit freedom. If \(W(t)=I_S\oplus V_E(t)\) is a bath unitary with \(W(0)=I\), then \(\widehat U=WU\) retains the same system block and final vacuum amplitude, but

\[
\boxed{
\widehat h=i\dot W W^\dagger+Wh_{\mathrm{tot},N}W^\dagger.
}
\]

So the prescribed transfer fixes its reduced generator, while additional choices determine the full microscopic energy operator. **Establishing a useful correspondence between that operator and the theta source spectrum is the energy-meaning question.**

I saved the derivation, including conventions and finite-scope qualifications, in [Note07](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/07_positive_theta_primitives/01_jensen/01_mellin_curvature/08_open_quantum_dynamics/brainstorm/notes/07_HAMILTONIAN_CONSTRUCTION_EQUATIONS_20261103.md).

Let's seperate the earlier results from this discussion. The basic assertions in the equations you wrote about the evolution say that H is related to G through being its Hermitian part, R_N being the anti-Hermitian part (or vice versa), and G_N being the sum of the two. That is vacuous.

What I want is a relationship between the actual states that are represented through the transfer K. I think we've diverged from that.
I’ll set aside the Hamiltonian split and return to the states on either side of \(K\). I’ll distinguish what the transfer actually relates from what the energy model would still need to explain.

The original identity makes the distinction clear: \(K_{ij}\) encodes overlaps between two theta-derived orbital families. The activity parameter rescales those orbitals but leaves their individually normalized wavefunctions unchanged. So interpreting \(v\) as time adds a realization; it does not establish evolution between the original source states.

You’re right. I answered **“how can the prescribed \(K\) be realized dynamically?”** when you were asking **“what relationship connects the states represented through \(K\)?”** The decomposition of \(G\) does not answer that question.

The original states come from two families of wavefunctions in \(L^2((0,\infty),du)\):

\[
f_i(u)=\frac{\Phi^{(2i)}(u)}{\sqrt{\Phi(u)}},
\qquad
g_j(u)=\frac{u^{2j}\sqrt{\Phi(u)}}{(2j)!}.
\]

Both are constructed from the same theta source: one through derivatives, the other through moments. Their established relationship is

\[
\boxed{\langle f_i,g_j\rangle=c_{j-i}.}
\]

For several fermions, this becomes the actual overlap

\[
\boxed{
\left\langle
f_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge f_{i_r},
g_{j_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge g_{j_r}
\right\rangle
=\det[c_{j_b-i_a}].
}
\]

These wavefunctions generally have different norms and are not orthonormal. After normalizing the nonzero wedges,

\[
\langle\widehat F_I,\widehat G_J\rangle
=
\frac{\det[c_{j_b-i_a}]}
{\sqrt{\det M_I^f\,\det M_J^g}},
\]

where \(M_I^f\) and \(M_J^g\) are their respective Gram matrices.

**\(K\) encodes these overlaps in an orthonormal coefficient basis.** Specifically,

\[
\langle e_i,K_ve_j\rangle
=
\frac{v^{j-i}}{F(v)}c_{j-i}
=
\left\langle v^{-i}f_i,\frac{v^j}{F(v)}g_j\right\rangle.
\]

Equivalently, for finite lists, define

\[
A_ve_i=v^{-i}f_i,\qquad
B_ve_j=\frac{v^j}{F(v)}g_j.
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{K_{v,N}=A_v^\dagger B_v.}
\]

This is a matrix of overlaps between the two source-derived families. It does **not** establish a physical process carrying \(g_j\) into \(f_i\): \(A_v^\dagger\) is generally not \(A_v^{-1}\).

There is a particularly revealing consequence. For \(v>0\),

\[
\frac{A_ve_i}{\|A_ve_i\|}
=\frac{f_i}{\|f_i\|},
\qquad
\frac{B_ve_j}{\|B_ve_j\|}
=\frac{g_j}{\|g_j\|}.
\]

**The individually normalized original source states do not change with \(v\).** The apparent \(v\)-evolution of \(K_v\) belongs to the coefficient encoding; interpreting it as time was an additional modeling choice.

So the substantive question is how the common theta source—and potentially its energy spectrum—constrains the relationship between these derivative-prepared and moment-prepared states. We have their exact overlap formula. We have not established an additional energy-based relation explaining or controlling that overlap.

I’ve recorded this correction in [Note08](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/07_positive_theta_primitives/01_jensen/01_mellin_curvature/08_open_quantum_dynamics/brainstorm/notes/08_RETURN_TO_SOURCE_STATES_AND_TRANSFER_PAIRING_20261103.md). The earlier realization results remain separate; the current discussion returns to these source states.

When you wrote the wedge products down, it actually suggests a different interpretation then the quantum mechanical one. Earlier in the repo, I attached a paper that I wrote /shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-2/active/21_quaternion_theta_geometry/source-documents/QuaternionForms-Final.pdf.  Take a look at equation 2.3, with the Bochner Martinelli formula. Perhaps a similar trick could be used to write the overlap integrals as independent integrals with a kernel. What do you think about this?

Also, it sounds like the v evolution doesn't provide much utility based on your last comments, is that correct?
The paper was a draft and I never published it by the way

I’ll read equation 2.3 and check whether its kernel construction suggests a useful way to separate the overlap integrals. I’ll also reassess what the \(v\)-evolution contributes. I’ll refer to your paper as an unpublished draft.
I’m using the PDF skill to inspect the displayed formula and its assumptions; text extraction alone can miss signs and wedge ordering.

The analogy works for a finite-interval version of our overlaps: applying Cauchy reconstruction to both factors gives an exact double contour integral with an explicit kernel. This follows the construction behind equation 2.3, while preserving our real-line integration measure. I also agree that \(v\)-dynamics is secondary to this question: changing \(v>0\) changes neither the determinant signs nor the neighboring-amplitude ratio.

The wedge products also separate: the two source determinants acquire their own contour variables, and the coupling becomes the determinant of the one-particle kernel. That gives a concrete analytic route to examine. The open question is whether its kernel or contour structure yields a new bound; the exact representation alone does not settle the sign.

**Yes—the reconstruction idea in equation 2.3 applies naturally to the source-state pairing, and an exact finite-interval version can be written down.** I inspected pages 2–3 of your **unpublished February 2014 draft**. :codex-file-citation{path="/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-2/active/21_quaternion_theta_geometry/source-documents/QuaternionForms-Final.pdf" purpose="source"}

Your construction has the structure

\[
\int_\Omega\omega\wedge\nu
=
C_n\int_{\partial\Omega}\int_{\partial\Omega}
\omega(z)\wedge K_n(z,w)\wedge\nu(w).
\]

The useful mechanism is to reconstruct each factor separately, then integrate their shared original variable into a coupling kernel. We can follow that mechanism for our real-line overlaps without importing the draft’s particular Bochner–Martinelli kernel unchanged.

Our pairing is

\[
\langle f_i,g_j\rangle
=\int_0^\infty
\Phi^{(2i)}(u)\frac{u^{2j}}{(2j)!}\,du.
\]

The square-root factors have canceled. Write

\[
a_i(u)=\Phi^{(2i)}(u),\qquad
b_j(u)=\frac{u^{2j}}{(2j)!},
\qquad
M_{ij}^{R}=\int_0^R a_i(u)b_j(u)\,du.
\]

For fixed \(R\), choose positively oriented contours enclosing \([0,R]\) within the source’s holomorphy strip \(|\operatorname{Im}z|<\pi/8\). Applying [Cauchy’s formula](https://dlmf.nist.gov/1.9.E30) separately to both factors gives

\[
\boxed{
M_{ij}^{R}
=
\oint_{\Gamma_z}\oint_{\Gamma_w}
a_i(z)\,\mathcal H_R(z,w)\,b_j(w)
\frac{dw}{2\pi i}\frac{dz}{2\pi i}.
}
\]

The kernel is explicit:

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal H_R(z,w)
=\int_0^R\frac{du}{(z-u)(w-u)}
=\frac{\ell_R(z)-\ell_R(w)}{w-z},
\qquad
\ell_R(z)=\log\frac{z}{z-R}.
}
\]

The defining integral fixes the logarithm branch. Its apparent diagonal singularity is removable:

\[
\mathcal H_R(z,z)=\frac{R}{z(z-R)}.
\]

**This supplies the separation you suggested:** the derivative-derived source factor depends on \(z\), the moment-derived factor depends on \(w\), and the kernel couples them.

The wedge products inherit the same structure. With

\[
\mathcal A_I(\mathbf z)=\det[a_{i_a}(z_c)],
\qquad
\mathcal B_J(\mathbf w)=\det[b_{j_b}(w_d)],
\]

two determinant expansions give

\[
\boxed{
\det[M^R_{i_a j_b}]
=
\frac1{(r!)^2}
\oint_{\Gamma_z^r}\oint_{\Gamma_w^r}
\mathcal A_I(\mathbf z)\,
\det[\mathcal H_R(z_c,w_d)]\,
\mathcal B_J(\mathbf w)
\prod_c\frac{dz_c}{2\pi i}
\prod_d\frac{dw_d}{2\pi i}.
}
\]

So the coupling between the two exterior products is itself a determinant kernel. This is a classical analytic interpretation of the overlap.

The remaining research question is whether this representation exposes a useful **kernel property, contour geometry, or cancellation**. The formula alone does not establish the sign. Also, although \(M_{ij}^R\to c_{j-i}\) at fixed indices as \(R\to\infty\), an unbounded-contour version must retain and justify its boundary and tail terms. I have not discarded them.

On \(v\), **for this source-state question, I agree that its evolution is secondary.** Its established utility is organizing a normalized bounded transfer:

\[
K_v=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{c_nv^n}{F(v)}S^n.
\]

But the amplitudes satisfy

\[
A_{I,J}(v)
=\frac{v^{\sum J-\sum I}}{F(v)^r}\det[c_{j_b-i_a}],
\]

so their signs are independent of \(v>0\). The relevant neighboring-amplitude ratio is also exactly \(v\)-independent. This does not exclude a useful estimate at a convenient \(v\), but the constructed evolution has supplied no new control of that ratio so far.

**I would pursue your kernel proposal directly from the original source pairings, holding \(v\) fixed or omitting it.** I saved the derivation and its limitations in [Note09](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/07_positive_theta_primitives/01_jensen/01_mellin_curvature/08_open_quantum_dynamics/brainstorm/notes/09_SEPARATED_CONTOUR_KERNEL_FOR_SOURCE_OVERLAPS_20261103.md).

**Next: [B] MC08-B03 — Astra:** examine one concrete source/kernel property that could yield an additional bound.

Can you create a new subfolder within 01_mellin_curvature to work on this, and write these results into a draft research-overview without creating the research plan part of that document or the research progress file yet? Can you also create a README for the new folder? I want to also explore the Hamiltonian picture further, so it will be good to separate out this investigation.
